inputs.name: value

nodes.title: Text Encoder
widgets_values:
This node loads our text encoder and is the starting point of the workflow. The "CLIP" naming is a limitation of ComfyUI. CLIPs are not technically the same thing as text encoders in this context.

Text encoders are highly specialised translators and are defined at the point where the LLM itself is trained. The way the LLM is trained, the way it is presented data during its training, is the same embedding formatting that is later used to talk to it. Essentially, it takes our natural language input and transforms it into embeddings the model can understand.

nodes.title: minimax_music3_text_encoder
widgets_values:
To help explain the file names, I've created another node for this same workflow below. The encoder above is 8.9GB, whereas the one below is 10.6GB. They're the same model, only the one above has been quantized more than the one below. See the main explanation sections overhead for more info on this.

Both file names begin "minimax_music3_", this is the family of models they belong to, often includes the developers name and/or a generation name. Think of this like ChatGPT 5.6 or Claude Opus, it's the Minimax family, specifically the music3 model.

Each file then explicitly states it's role, "text_encoder", makes it very clear what these do.

Now we have divergence, model above "pruned_int8" vs below "fp8". As mentioned above, the model actually hooked into this workflow is quantized to enable faster generation, the model below is technically compressed too, but to a less significant degree. The subject of compression/quantization gets complex fast, if you wish to understand it further please look at the main explanation notes overhead where I dive into the detail more.

Again our file names differ, above we have "convrot" and below we have "e4m3fn". These are the compression algorithms used to reach the level of quantization each model has been compressed to. Meaning there may be several different INT8 and FP8 variants available where individuals have used different algorithms to compress. I have personally yet to find any reason to worry about one algorithm being better than another.

And finally ".safetensors", the file format. More on this in the main explanation notes overhead.

Each track has a song underneath it, both songs were generated with the exact same seed and configuration, the only difference is the text encoder used. Have a listen to each and see if you can spot the difference!

inputs.label: How can one number be more precise than another?
inputs.name: value

nodes.title: Precision
widgets_values:
Precision defines how accurately, and over what numerical range, the model's values can be represented, how many pages it has in its book of knowledge.

When looking at precision we're usually looking at precision values that are Floating Points or Brain-floating Points. With levels of FP32, FP16, BF16 or INT8 most typically seen.

Imagine we're in a workshop, we need to measure something, on the table infront of us is an assortment of rulers.

Some rulers are longer than others, some rules measure in centimetres, others in millimetres. Each ruler has a fixed range of tasks it is able to complete, a  10cm long ruler can't measure a 20cm long item, a measurement needed in millimetres can't accurately be taken in centimetres.

The numeric value on our precision level signifies how many digits each vector is in length, an FP32 vector is expressed over 32 digits, an INT8 vector is expressed over 8 digits.

Sadly, precision is not simple enough to stop there.

These are exponential values, meaning the computer does not use all of those bits simply to write out one long number. Instead, a floating-point value is split into separate parts: a sign, an exponent, and a fraction.

This is similar to scientific notation. Instead of writing 120,000, we could write 1.2 × 10⁵. The 1.2 provides the precise value, while the 10⁵ determines its scale. Computers do essentially the same thing, except they work in binary, so the scale is based on powers of 2 rather than powers of 10.

For example, the same basic value can be moved across vastly different scales:

a. 1.25 × 2⁻³  = 0.15625
b. 1.25 × 2⁰   = 1.25
c. 1.25 × 2³   = 10
d. 1.25 × 2¹⁰  = 1280

The exponent therefore controls the length of our ruler, determining the range of values it can represent. The fraction controls how finely marked that ruler is, determining how precisely values within that range can be represented.

This is why two 16-bit formats can behave very differently. FP16 gives more of its available bits to the fraction, producing finer measurements, but fewer to the exponent, giving it a smaller overall range. BF16 does the opposite: it uses the same 8-bit exponent as FP32, giving it a similarly enormous range, but has fewer fraction bits and therefore coarser precision.

nodes.title: Weights
widgets_values:
Weights are the numerical parameters learned during training.

More weights, more capacity. What the model learns depends on its training.


They determine how strongly different pieces of information influence one another as data passes through the model.

A trained model may contain millions, billions or now even trillions of these values, and the model file primarily exists to store them.

More weight, more knowledge.

nodes.title: Tokenizer
widgets_values:
Before text reaches the text encoder, a tokenizer breaks it into smaller units called tokens. A token may represent a whole word, part of a word, punctuation or another recurring text pattern.

The tokenizer used during inference generally needs to match the one the encoder was trained with, because changing how text is divided changes what numerical inputs the model receives.

You may have heard of "tokens" if you've ever looked at purchasing an AI subscription or API access, this is one of the more common ways to commercialise AI models, by billing the user based on the number of tokens they consume.

nodes.title: Embeddings / Conditioning
widgets_values:
An embedding is the numerical representation of information.

It is the output of the text encoder.

A text encoder converts words and phrases into arrays of numbers (vectors) that represent their meaning and relationships. These embeddings are then supplied to the generation model as conditioning, guiding what it produces without passing the original text directly into the model.

nodes.title: File Types
widgets_values:
mlx
lora

There are many file types, or references to groups of files that you'll come across when running AI models. It can be confusing at first, hopefully what you've read so far, and what you'll read further along will help piece together the jigsaw so that these terms and types make sense.

At it's core, there are three main types of model file we're concerned with for workflows such as this, those being:

1. UNet (DiT), this is our work horse. These are neural networking models which when graphed are typically U shaped, a large input comes in, it is compressed down and understood by the machine in its base form and then uncompressed back to full size for return to the human operator. Also referred to as DiT, or Diffusion Transformer, it is the very basis of the current world of AI we're using. A generation is born out of pure noise and refined, or diffused, until it resembles the planned output.

2. Text Encoder, the interpreter between the humans input and the UNets engine.

3. VAE, similar to a text encoder, the VAE receives the output of the UNet and assembles the vectors into the final form before handing it back to the human.

These items may be packaged individually, as they are in this workflow or they may be packaged together in a single file called a Checkpoint.

The formats these items are typically found in are .safetensors and .gguf.

These are the file types used to save, compress, and read those models on your storage drive.

Safetensors: This is the modern industry standard format for saving AI weights. It is highly secure (cannot hide malicious computer viruses like older .ckpt files could) and loads into your computer's memory incredibly fast.

GGUF: This is a specialized compression format. While standard .safetensors files usually store models in high precision (FP16 or FP32), GGUF squishes the file size down (Quantization) to Q4, Q5, or Q8. This allows you to run massive "engines" on cheaper consumer graphics cards without losing much quality.

Specialisations

There are other outlying file types or quantizations which are typically very specific to the workflow being ran. Neither are being used within this workflow, but it is worth being aware of them as they are very common.

MLX: This is an open-source machine learning framework built by Apple specifically for Apple Silicon (M1, M2, M3, M4 chips). Think of it as a specialized fuel efficient engine mapping tuned specifically for Mac hardware, bypassing standard Windows/Nvidia-centric tools.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation): This is an aftermarket modification or "plugin" (like adding a custom spoiler or turbocharger). Instead of retraining a massive 20GB checkpoint to learn a new art style or specific character, you train a tiny 100MB LoRA file and inject it into the UNet while it runs.

nodes.title: Large Language Model
widgets_values:
Here we are, the beating heart of this workflow, whilst this does NOT make our song it is the most important component of this entire workflow.

You can change model precisions all day long, but what's written above will drive the quality of your final output more than any increase in parameter count can.

This is the LLM (Large Language Model), we feed it a caption and a lyric set, it will take that natural language information and process it into an exact description of how the song should sound (based on its training) which gets passed to our sampler for generation in the form of structured conditioning.

So, what do we tell it?

Caption:

Lyrics:

A few other variables available:

Seed: 
The starting point for diffusion, think of it as a ball in a bingo wheel. It's starting point would be the seed, then through the diffusion process the wheel turns and the ball moves through the wheel until the wheel stops. It's seemingly random, almost impossible to predict where it will end and the ball it started next to could finish in the opposite position. This may sound like a variable of little use, but if you find a seed the leads to your bingo ball getting picked (i.e. the seed produces a good song structure), then you can reliably repeat generations of the same song adjusting other variables, captions or lyrics to fine tune the final product. It is hard to overstate the importance of tracking seeds!

Max Duration: 
With this specific model, we don't define an exact track time, only a maximum and the model will generate a track that lasts up to the maximum boundary based on what it calculates to be the ideal BPM et al.

CFG Scale:
CFG (Classifier-Free Guidance) controls prompt adherence. Think of it as the parents of the AI model as its working. Lower CFG values would be those parents after a long day of work, maybe a bottle or two, half keeping an eye on their child as it plays with matches. Higher CFG values, same parents, but their parents are coming over for dinner, they're in full "eyes in the back of my head" mode, nothing goes uncorrected, that child will have to do whatever they say.

CFG is a tough variable to get right and likely one of the ones you'll find yourself adjusting and doubting yourself over the effect being a net positive or negative.

For this model in particular, CFG 1.7 is about the sweet spot, however I have found when working on tracks that are supposed to sound a little more vintage or like they're playing off a cassette a CFG of 1.2 can make the experience feel more authentic.

You can read more here: https://comfyui.nomadoor.net/en/ai-capabilities/cfg/

Top K:
Top K sampling controls the range of vectors that are available per token. Imagine you 'had' the number 100 and I told you that you can choose any number either side of 100 +/- 50, you effectively have 100 values you can pick. It may work well that you can pick such a wide range, or I may find that actually I need you to stick closer to the origin point, so I adjust the Top K value down to 10 and now your range is dramatically reduced and more predictable.

Top K controls the LLMs ability to control variation. As it is searching its probabilistic dictionary, this parameter controls how 'far' it is allowed to look away from its origin point. Higher values will produce greater levels of creative insanity, lower levels will be more locked in and perhaps mundane. Throughout my testing with MiniMax I have found zero value in changing this from 50.

nodes.title: Example of a completed prompt
widgets_values:
Global Metadata

Minimal mid-2010s alternative rap and spacey trap with an underground UK feel. Slow, heavy half-time bounce around 68–70 BPM, or approximately 136–140 BPM in double-time counting. Keep the production sparse, repetitive and hypnotic rather than constantly evolving: rounded sub-bass, dry punchy kick, tight snare, simple crisp hi-hats, restrained trap percussion and a small eerie synthetic motif repeating through most of the track. Harmony should remain minimal and loop-based, creating a slightly sinister but playful nocturnal atmosphere. The groove should feel relaxed and confident despite the fast vocal phrasing. Preserve substantial empty space around the vocal. Avoid hyperpop maximalism, glitch-heavy production, dramatic drops, dense synth layers, EDM effects, rock instrumentation and excessive transitional sound design.

Vocal Details

Female lead vocal with a youthful, bright, slightly nasal timbre and clear British-accented rap delivery. Performance is cheeky, dry, provocative and self-assured rather than manic. Verses use tightly articulated conversational rap with quick internal rhymes and playful changes of emphasis, but maintain a steady underlying cadence. Pre-choruses become slightly more melodic and sing-song without turning into full pop singing. Choruses are deliberately tiny and repetitive, delivered as a catchy chant with light doubling rather than a huge layered hook. Keep the lead close, dry and intelligible. Use only occasional restrained ad-libs or doubles; avoid constant vocal warping, exaggerated character voices and disruptive effects.

Arrangement

[intro]

Establish the core bass, drum and eerie synth loop immediately

[verse]

Bring the full established groove into place without. Keep the backing repetitive and spacious.

[chorus]

Maintain essentially the same groove. Introduce the short repeated chant with light vocal doubling and a modest increase in bass and drum weight, but avoid turning it into a large pop chorus.

[verse]

Return directly to the central loop. Keep the instrumental stable while the vocal becomes denser, quicker and more conversational, with brief ad-libs occupying the spaces between phrases.

[chorus]

Restore the established chant essentially unchanged. Preserve its repetition and familiarity rather than increasing the scale.

[verse]

Maintain the same central groove while the tongue-twisting vocal patterns become increasingly intricate. Keep the beat relaxed underneath the faster articulation and preserve clear empty space around the lead.

[chorus]

Repeat the established chorus with the doubling and modest rhythmic reinforcement.

[verse]

the vocal complexity increases further. Allow increasingly compressed phrasing, rapid consonants and call-and-response ad-libs to create the sense of acceleration without changing the underlying tempo.

[chorus]

Return once more to the familiar chant, providing a simple rhythmic reset before the final escalation.

[verse]

Treat the final extended verse as the vocal and rhythmic climax. Begin over the established groove, then progressively tighten the vocal spacing as the multi-syllabic words and repeated place names accumulate. Allow the delivery to become increasingly rapid and relentless while keeping articulation clear. The drums may gain slightly stronger hi-hat activity and percussion toward the end, but the core bass and eerie synth loop should remain unchanged. Avoid a dramatic drop or large instrumental build; the escalating vocal itself should create the climax.

[outro]

Strip the groove back slightly beneath the final short word permutations. Return to the loose, playful spacing of the opening, using bass, percussion and the established synth motif. End abruptly and simply after the final vocal response rather than building toward a conventional musical resolution.

widgets_values_named.caption:
Global Metadata

Minimal mid-2010s alternative rap and spacey trap with an underground UK feel. Slow, heavy half-time bounce around 68–70 BPM, or approximately 136–140 BPM in double-time counting. Keep the production sparse, repetitive and hypnotic rather than constantly evolving: rounded sub-bass, dry punchy kick, tight snare, simple crisp hi-hats, restrained trap percussion and a small eerie synthetic motif repeating through most of the track. Harmony should remain minimal and loop-based, creating a slightly sinister but playful nocturnal atmosphere. The groove should feel relaxed and confident despite the fast vocal phrasing. Preserve substantial empty space around the vocal. Avoid hyperpop maximalism, glitch-heavy production, dramatic drops, dense synth layers, EDM effects, rock instrumentation and excessive transitional sound design.

Vocal Details

Female lead vocal with a youthful, bright, slightly nasal timbre and clear British-accented rap delivery. Performance is cheeky, dry, provocative and self-assured rather than manic. Verses use tightly articulated conversational rap with quick internal rhymes and playful changes of emphasis, but maintain a steady underlying cadence. Pre-choruses become slightly more melodic and sing-song without turning into full pop singing. Choruses are deliberately tiny and repetitive, delivered as a catchy chant with light doubling rather than a huge layered hook. Keep the lead close, dry and intelligible. Use only occasional restrained ad-libs or doubles; avoid constant vocal warping, exaggerated character voices and disruptive effects.

Arrangement

[intro]

Establish the core bass, drum and eerie synth loop immediately

[verse]

Bring the full established groove into place without. Keep the backing repetitive and spacious.

[chorus]

Maintain essentially the same groove. Introduce the short repeated chant with light vocal doubling and a modest increase in bass and drum weight, but avoid turning it into a large pop chorus.

[verse]

Return directly to the central loop. Keep the instrumental stable while the vocal becomes denser, quicker and more conversational, with brief ad-libs occupying the spaces between phrases.

[chorus]

Restore the established chant essentially unchanged. Preserve its repetition and familiarity rather than increasing the scale.

[verse]

Maintain the same central groove while the tongue-twisting vocal patterns become increasingly intricate. Keep the beat relaxed underneath the faster articulation and preserve clear empty space around the lead.

[chorus]

Repeat the established chorus with the doubling and modest rhythmic reinforcement.

[verse]

the vocal complexity increases further. Allow increasingly compressed phrasing, rapid consonants and call-and-response ad-libs to create the sense of acceleration without changing the underlying tempo.

[chorus]

Return once more to the familiar chant, providing a simple rhythmic reset before the final escalation.

[verse]

Treat the final extended verse as the vocal and rhythmic climax. Begin over the established groove, then progressively tighten the vocal spacing as the multi-syllabic words and repeated place names accumulate. Allow the delivery to become increasingly rapid and relentless while keeping articulation clear. The drums may gain slightly stronger hi-hat activity and percussion toward the end, but the core bass and eerie synth loop should remain unchanged. Avoid a dramatic drop or large instrumental build; the escalating vocal itself should create the climax.

[outro]

Strip the groove back slightly beneath the final short word permutations. Return to the loose, playful spacing of the opening, using bass, percussion and the established synth motif. End abruptly and simply after the final vocal response rather than building toward a conventional musical resolution.

nodes.title: Sampler
widgets_values:
The sampler is where our actual song is built.

We've taken our input prompt, converted it to the embeddings via our text encoder, passed it through our LLM to generate exact direction on what the song should be and now the diffusion model will turn that direction into a real song (almost).

There are once again a set of parameters used to control the sampler, some will be familiar by now.

Seed
The function of this seed is identical to the the one found in our LLM step, in this workflow it has significantly less impact on the final song output as the direction built by the LLM is largely what drives this workflow.

Steps
The value entered here has the biggest impact upon generation time (assuming you're not offloading your model weights!) as it controls the number of passes the sampler will make over the latent object. Each additional step adds another full pass. There is a clear correlation between number of steps and quality of the final output supplied by the sampler. However, that doesn't mean you should crank the steps way up and wait for pure gold... in the case of this workflow, it's relatively harmless to use a high step count, but in my testing anything over 40 steps offered little noticeable improvement in quality. 

Some models and workflows will be harmed by step counts being too high and result in overprocessing of the latent object, always check what advice is given for the a specific model/workflow and fine tune it from there.

CFG
The function of this CFG is identical to the the one found in our LLM step, in this workflow it has significantly less impact on the final song output as the direction built by the LLM is largely what drives this workflow.

You can read more here: https://comfyui.nomadoor.net/en/ai-capabilities/cfg/

Sampler Name
Sampling controls how diffusion is run. As mentioned above, the diffusion process is ran in steps, the model passes over the latent object repeatedly until the defined number of steps is reached. Each pass reduces noise from the previous, refining the generation. The sampler determines how that denoising is applied within each step.

Scheduler
The scheduler is responsible for determining how each step is controlled, in other words, in step 1 we want to be aggressive and reduce noise in big sweeping passes, but by the time we hit step 15 we want to take smaller reductions, more fine tuned and surgical.

There are a large number of scheduler algorithms available and I won't pretend to understand the inner workings of them, but "simple" is a commonly used scheduler across many types of diffusion workflow and it works very well with this workflow.

You can read more here: https://comfyui.nomadoor.net/en/ai-capabilities/sampling/

Denoise

nodes.title: Conditioning
widgets_values:
Our LLM gives us the conditioning that we use to drive our sampler and "seconds" which we'll talk about below.

Conditioning
Conditioning is the instruction the LLM has made, based off our prompt, which will drive the sampler to build the song we've asked for. Many samplers require a positive and a negative conditioning set. Positive being what we do want and negative being what we don't want.

However, not all diffusion models are built to work from positive/negative prompting, such as Minimax which is single prompt driven. The presence of the negative zero conditioning in this workflow is purely due to ComfyUI/node design limitations, we can't run the sampler without connecting something to its negative input.

Seconds
Typically a workflow would just supply the latent object immediately, however with this being a music generation workflow more control is desired over track duration. When we feed our sampler the conditioning, it needs to apply diffusion to the latent object until we reach our step limit (if that's confusing, wait till the next node set, it'll all get cleared up).

In order to 'shape' the track correctly, we need to ensure the latent object it denoises is already the correct size for our track. Therefore, we pre-define the maximum length again and hand it that latent ready for shaping. We're creating a blank basically.

You can read more here: https://comfyui.nomadoor.net/en/ai-capabilities/conditioning/

nodes.title: The Diffusion Model
widgets_values:
This node to the left loads the diffusion model.

Significantly smaller than our text encoder, this model is approx. 4.7GB, meaning it very comfortably fits onto my home GPU with no offloading required.

As mentioned, this workflow is really driven by the text encoder, a very top-down hierarchy where this diffusion model is just doing largely what it's been told to do.

Other workflows are the opposite way around, where the sampling process using the diffusion model is the true driver of the final output.

nodes.title: Variational Autoencoder (VAE
widgets_values:
The VAE is our final process within this workflow.

VAEs operate similar to text encoders, in that they're largely translation tools transforming objects into/out-of embeddings, however VAEs are used for non-text objects.

In the case of this workflow, we're transforming our now denoised and refined latent into an actual audio file.

Other workflows, such as those for modifying existing audio would use a VAE encoder earlier in the workflow to take that existing audio and translate it into embeddings for the LLM or sampler to reference. 

In these workflows, it would be the same VAE typically that encodes and decodes, however this model family does not work from reference music so the VAE supplied is a decoder only.

Once we've decoded, we have a single audio output which we supply into a node that saves our track in the location and format desired.

And that's it, it's that simple to end humanities creativity...

nodes.title: Variational Autoencoder (VAE
widgets_values:
VAE files are often the smallest sized within a diffusion workflow.

This VAE for example is only 211MB, so 50+ times smaller than the FP8 text encoder we talked about at the start of this workflow.

For this reason, it is extremely uncommon to find quantized VAE models.

As with the previous models, we have the model family included in the name, "minimax_music3_" and the file type is again .safetensors. The new element here is "dav" which tells us it is meant for audio.

"dav" meaning "Decoder-Audio-VAE"
